item.title: Profile-guided LLVM Optimization
item.description:
Modern processors are incredibly fast, but memory latency remains a major bottleneck for performance. Compiler optimizations that restructure code to improve cache behavior and instruction efficiency can have a significant impact. In this project, I explored and implemented two profile-guided optimizations within the LLVM compiler framework.

Both techniques use dynamic profiling information to make more informed, speculative decisions during compilation—targeting performance gains that go beyond traditional static analysis.

Frequent Path Loop-Invariant Code Motion (FPLICM)

Traditional LICM hoists loop-invariant instructions outside of loops to avoid redundant computations. However, it must guarantee correctness across all paths within a loop, often leaving optimization opportunities untapped.

FPLICM builds on this by identifying instructions that are invariant along the most frequent execution path, even if they vary on rare paths. These “almost invariant” instructions are speculatively hoisted based on profiling data. If the program later takes an infrequent path, a lightweight repair mechanism ensures correctness by re-executing the hoisted code.

This speculative approach increases optimization aggressiveness while preserving correctness, leveraging the observation that most programs exhibit strong execution locality in loops.

Profile-Guided Software Prefetching

To address cache miss latency, I developed a profile-guided software prefetching pass. Unlike static approaches that require manually tuning prefetch distances, this optimization utilizes profile information from Intel’s Last Branch Record (LBR) to determine the best prefetch distance and prefetch injection site.

In testing, this technique improved performance effectively, especially for loops with indirect memory accesses—cases where hardware prefetchers typically fall short.
